vignette:
Mr. Singh is a 76-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his life working as an electrician in a bustling city. He has always taken pride in his craft, often reflecting on the satisfaction that comes from fixing a broken fixture or wiring a new home. His work, which he continues to do part-time, has kept him engaged with the community and provided him with a sense of purpose. However, a recent traumatic event has cast a shadow over his once vibrant spirit.

It was a warm evening in late summer when Mr. Singh’s life took a harrowing turn. He had just finished a small job at a nearby house and was walking home, tools in hand, when he was approached by two young men. At first, he felt a flicker of annoyance at their boisterous laughter, but that quickly shifted to fear as they demanded his wallet. Although he is not a confrontational man, Mr. Singh remembers feeling a surge of anger mixed with panic; he was not one to back down easily. He tightened his grip on his tools, thinking of using them for defense, but before he could react, one of the assailants shoved him to the ground. The sudden impact knocked the air from his lungs, and in that moment, he felt utterly powerless. His heart raced as they rifled through his pockets, taking not just his money but a sense of safety he had held onto for decades.

In the days following the mugging, Mr. Singh struggles to find his footing. He grows increasingly withdrawn, spending long hours sitting silently on the porch of his home, watching the world pass by but feeling detached from it. His wife, Tara, notices his distant demeanor. She tries to coax him into conversation, to bring back the jovial man who would share stories of his workday over dinner. But Mr. Singh finds it difficult to express the turmoil brewing inside him. Instead, he smiles weakly, offering her reassurances that he is fine, even as he feels a knot tightening in his chest.

As weeks turn into months, the memories of that night become a relentless echo in his mind. Mr. Singh often relives the moment he was knocked down, the cold concrete against his back, the feeling of helplessness as he watched his belongings vanish into the night. He begins to experience nightmares that wake him in a cold sweat, the shadows of his attackers looming large in his dreams. Each time he closes his eyes, he is transported back to that moment, and it feels as though he is living it all over again. The fear remains palpable, and he wrestles with it daily.

His work as an electrician, once a source of pride and connection, becomes increasingly daunting. He finds himself avoiding jobs in neighborhoods that remind him of the mugging, fearing that he might encounter danger again. The once-familiar streets now seem ominous, filled with potential threats lurking behind every corner. Mr. Singh’s concentration wanes; he fumbles with his tools, hesitating to climb ladders or navigate tight spaces. He worries that he is becoming a burden to his coworkers, who rely on his expertise. The very thing he loved now feels like a reminder of his vulnerability, and he wonders if it’s time to retire for good.

At home, the emotional toll weighs heavily on his relationship with Tara. She tries to reach out, but he often brushes her off, feeling ashamed of his fear. He grieves the man he used to be—the confident, capable electrician who could tackle any job and any challenge. Instead, he feels like a shadow of himself, lost in a fog of anxiety and dread. The laughter that once filled their home has turned into silence, and he longs for the warmth of connection that seems just out of reach.

While Mr. Singh continues to navigate his daily life, the world outside feels increasingly hostile, and he fights to reclaim his sense of safety and self. Unbeknownst to him, the journey of healing is just beginning, and the path ahead remains uncertain. But each day, he takes small steps, clinging to the hope that one day he will find a way to feel secure in his own skin again.
